The day went much like the one before. Mrs. Hurst and Miss Bingley spent several hours that morning with the patient, who continued to improve, though slowly. In the evening Elizabeth joined the others in the drawing-room. This time, however, they did not bring out the table for loo. Mr. Darcy was writing a letter. Miss Bingley sat nearby, watching his progress and repeatedly interrupting him with messages for his sister. Mr. Hurst and Mr. Bingley were playing piquet, while Mrs. Hurst watched their game.

Elizabeth picked up some sewing and found plenty to amuse her in the conversation between Darcy and his companion. The lady constantly praised his handwriting, the straightness of his lines, or the length of his letter. He received every compliment with complete indifference. It made a curious exchange, and fitted Elizabeth’s opinion of them both exactly.

“How pleased Miss Darcy will be to receive a letter like that!”

He did not reply.

“You write exceptionally quickly.”

“You are mistaken. I write quite slowly.”

“You must have so many letters to write in a year! Business letters, too! I should find them dreadful!”

“Then it is fortunate that I have to write them, and you do not.”

“Please tell your sister how much I want to see her.”

“I have already told her once, as you asked.”

“I am afraid your pen isn’t pleasing you. Let me sharpen it for you. I am remarkably good at sharpening pens.”

“Thank you, but I always attend to my own.”

“How do you manage to keep your writing so straight?”

He said nothing.

“Tell your sister I am delighted to hear how much her harp playing has improved. And please tell her I am absolutely enchanted by her beautiful little design for a table. I think it is far better than Miss Grantley’s.”

“May I save your enthusiasm for my next letter? I have no room left to describe it properly.”

“Oh, it does not matter. I shall see her in January. But do you always write her such lovely long letters, Mr. Darcy?”

“They are usually long. Whether they are always lovely is for someone else to judge.”

“I always believe that anyone who can write a long letter easily must write well.”

“That won’t serve as a compliment to Darcy, Caroline,” her brother called out, “because writing does not come easily to him. He spends too long searching for words with four syllables. Don’t you, Darcy?”

“My way of writing is very different from yours.”

“Oh,” exclaimed Miss Bingley, “Charles writes as carelessly as anyone possibly could.

Not every one would have persisted so kindly as she did, and declined to accept Jane’s answer; but yesterday she declared positively that she would write no such refusal as Jane desired. She would wait—and indeed, by yesterday evening it was decided that Jane should go. Such a surprise to me! I had not the smallest notion! Jane drew Mrs. Elton aside and told her directly that, having considered the advantages of the place with Mrs. Smallridge, she had resolved to accept it. I knew nothing whatever until the whole affair was settled.”

“You passed the evening at Mrs. Elton’s?”

“Yes, every one of us; Mrs. Elton insisted upon our coming. We arranged it on the hill, as we were strolling with Mr. Knightley. ‘You must all come to us this evening,’ she said—‘I absolutely insist on having you all.’”

“Then Mr. Knightley was there also?”

“No, Mr. Knightley was not; he refused from the outset. I thought he would come, for Mrs. Elton declared she would not excuse him, but he never appeared. My mother, Jane, and I were all present, however, and passed a most agreeable evening. With such kind friends, Miss Woodhouse, one cannot fail to be agreeable, although every one appeared somewhat exhausted by the morning’s excursion. Pleasure itself is tiring, you know—and I cannot pretend that any of them seemed to have enjoyed it particularly. Nevertheless, I shall always remember it as a very pleasant party, and remain exceedingly grateful to the kind friends who asked me to join them.”

“Miss Fairfax had probably been reaching her decision throughout the day, though you knew nothing of it?”

“I dare say that is so.”

“Whenever the moment arrives, it must be painful to her and to all her friends. But I hope her situation will offer every possible comfort—I mean in the family’s character and manners.”

“Thank you, my dear Miss Woodhouse. Indeed, yes; everything imaginable is there to make her happy. Apart from the Sucklings and the Bragges, Mrs. Elton knows no other nursery establishment so generous and so elegant. Mrs. Smallridge is a most charming woman! Their manner of living is nearly equal to Maple Grove. As for the children, excepting the little Sucklings and little Bragges, nowhere could one find such refined, sweet children. Jane will receive such consideration and kindness! It will be all enjoyment, a life entirely of pleasure. And her salary! I really dare not tell you the amount of her salary, Miss Woodhouse.

No letter of sympathy had been sent to Ireland. Those responsible had paid for this neglect: when poor Lady Elliot herself died, no letter of sympathy arrived at Kellynch. There was therefore every reason to fear that the Dalrymples considered the family connection at an end. The anxious question was how to put matters right and be accepted as cousins again. Lady Russell and Mr Elliot, though more sensible about it, also thought it important. Family connections were always worth keeping, and good company always worth seeking. Lady Dalrymple had rented a house in Laura Place for three months and would live there in style. She had visited Bath the previous year, and Lady Russell had heard her described as a charming woman. They thought it very desirable to renew the connection, provided the Elliots could do so without losing their dignity.

Sir Walter, however, insisted on choosing his own method. At last he wrote his distinguished cousin an elaborate letter, full of explanations, regrets, and pleas. Neither Lady Russell nor Mr Elliot admired it, but it achieved everything he wanted. The Dowager Viscountess sent three hastily written lines in reply: she was very much honoured and would be happy to know them. The hard work was over; the pleasures could begin. They visited Laura Place and received the visiting cards of Dowager Viscountess Dalrymple and the Honourable Miss Carteret, which they could display wherever they would be most noticed. To everyone they spoke of “Our cousins in Laura Place” and “Our cousin, Lady Dalrymple, and Miss Carteret.”

Anne felt ashamed. Even if Lady Dalrymple and her daughter had been delightful, she would still have been embarrassed by all the excitement surrounding them. But there was nothing special about either of them. They had no outstanding manners, talents, or intelligence. Lady Dalrymple had earned her reputation as “a charming woman” simply by having a smile and a polite reply for everyone. Miss Carteret had even less to say. She was so plain and awkward that, without her high birth, she would never have been tolerated in Camden Place.

Lady Russell admitted that she had expected more. Still, she said, they were people worth knowing. When Anne ventured to tell Mr Elliot what she thought of them, he agreed that they had no particular merit themselves. Yet he maintained that they had value as relatives, as fashionable company, and as people who would attract other fashionable company. Anne smiled and said,

“My idea of good company, Mr Elliot, is to be with intelligent, well-informed people who have plenty to say. That is what I call good company.”
